nodes.title: From Frontier Models to Frugal Teams: Harnessing Domain Knowledge for Cost-Efficient Causal Discovery with AI Agents
nodes.abstract:
Motivation. Firms increasingly rely on causal structures, formalized as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), to uncover the causes and mechanisms underlying business outcomes, such as the drivers of demand, the sources of operational failures, and the pathways through which risks propagate through supply chain networks. Recovering these structures from observational data, a task known as causal discovery, is particularly difficult when the available observations are limited relative to the number and complexity of the relationships involved. Yet firms often possess substantial proprietary domain knowledge about the meaning, context, and plausible causal roles of the relevant variables. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) create a new opportunity to integrate such knowledge with observational evidence in causal discovery. However, available LLMs differ substantially in both capability and inference cost. Frontier models may reason more reliably about ambiguous or complex relationships, but relying on them throughout the discovery process can be prohibitively expensive at scale, whereas lower-cost models may be sufficient for many steps of the process but less reliable for others. The open question is therefore not whether stronger models improve causal discovery, but where in the process their additional capability is actually needed and worth its cost. We address this question by developing a multi-agent system for causal discovery that uses programmatic falsification tests to determine when a lower-cost model should seek guidance from a stronger model.

Methodology. We introduce CausalCascade, a two-agent AI system that treats model capability as a priced resource. The system operates through an iterative loop. In each iteration, a lower-cost Executor constructs or revises a candidate causal DAG using a structured knowledge base that captures domain context. A programmatic falsification module then tests the candidate DAG against observational data and returns structured feedback. When the feedback indicates a problem for which additional model capability may be valuable, the system invokes a more capable Advisor. The Advisor reads the current DAG, falsification results, and revision history from a shared context and returns a concise set of edge-level recommendations. The Executor uses the falsification feedback and, when available, the Advisor's recommendations to produce the next candidate DAG. The cycle continues until the system reaches the maximum number of iterations, at which point the Executor produces the final DAG. Successive graph versions, falsification results, and Advisor recommendations are logged, creating an auditable record of the discovery process.

We evaluate the system in collaboration with a leading North American telecommunications operator. The firm provided three proprietary causal DAGs (15, 30, and 57 nodes) sourced from its internal supply chain risk assessment. Together, the DAGs capture causal mechanisms at the market, procurement-category, and supplier levels. We treat these proprietary, expert-elicited DAGs as ground truth and generate small observational panels from them, allowing us to evaluate the accuracy of structure recovery while reducing concerns that the results are driven by memorization of public benchmark DAGs. In our implementation, we assign Claude Sonnet 4.6 to the Executor role and Claude Opus 4.8 to the Advisor role. Through controlled experiments, we compare CausalCascade with four classical causal-discovery algorithms (i.e., PC, GES, NOTEARS, and DAGMA), and two single-LLM baselines in which either the Executor model or the Advisor model performs the full discovery process alone.

Findings. CausalCascade and both single-LLM baselines recovered substantially more causal structure than the best classical algorithm across all three DAGs, demonstrating the value of incorporating domain knowledge when observational data is scarce. CausalCascade nearly matched the stronger LLM's average accuracy, achieving a mean F-score of 0.665 compared to 0.669 for the standalone stronger model, while incurring only 53% of its inference cost. CausalCascade achieved the highest F-score on two of the three DAGs. The Advisor's recommendations consistently improved the Executor's graph recovery. Complementary experiments using public benchmark DAGs supported that these results were not an artifact of benchmark memorization by the LLMs. The results also identified an important boundary condition: the Advisor was highly effective at removing or reorienting edges proposed by the Executor, but less reliable at proposing entirely missing edges. Consequently, the system is better suited for tasks where existing domain knowledge can yield a reasonably comprehensive initial graph.

Implications. This research provides a practical, scalable architecture for deploying AI in decision-critical causal discovery. We demonstrate that firms do not necessarily need to rely exclusively on their strongest models throughout the discovery process. By combining selective capability escalation with an auditable decision process, CausalCascade enables firms to manage inference costs efficiently while supporting governance, expert review, and organizational accountability by design. Broadly, this study highlights that organizational AI readiness depends not just on access to frontier models, but on the ability to provide AI agents with the right context and allocate reasoning capabilities where they generate the most value.

nodes.title: When Transparency Meets "AI Slop": The Effects of AI Labeling on Creator and Viewer Behavior on Pinterest
nodes.abstract: Generative AI has created new governance challenges for visual content platforms by making synthetic images easier to produce while raising concerns about authenticity, content quality, and user trust. This study examines the behavioral consequences of platform-enforced AI labeling on Pinterest. Using a longitudinal creator-week panel covering 9,706 creators and 1,474,552 Pins from December 2025 to April 2026, we estimate the effects of AI labeling on a propensity score matched sample. Our main approach employs a staggered difference-in-differences design using CSDID, with an interaction-weighted DID estimator as a robustness check. We find that AI labeling significantly reduces creators' weekly content production and follower growth. The main CSDID estimates imply a 16% decline in newly posted Pins and a 16.1% decline in new followers after labeling. In contrast, new comments and likes do not change significantly at the creator or Pin level. However, AI-related and negative AI-related comments increase by 0.3% and 0.2%, respectively, suggesting that the label makes AI somewhat more salient in audience discussion. Heterogeneity analyses show that although posting declines similarly across popularity groups, the follower-growth penalty is larger for more popular creators (18.6% vs. 9.9%). AI labeling also reduces new Pins by 15.5% and new followers by 13.3% among active creators, while estimates for inactive creators are not statistically significant. Potential platform mislabeling, as evaluated through human perception, is associated with significantly fewer subsequent Pins and lower follower growth. We also observe more consistent effects for inspired-to categories and stronger posting effects among creators whose Pins have greater potential for real-life implementation. These findings contribute to research on AI disclosure, platform governance, and creator economies by showing that platform-enforced AI labeling can reshape both audience reactions and creators' productivity.

nodes.title: Substantive vs Symbolic AI Disclosure and Subsequent Safety Risks & Performance: Evidence from US Public Pharmaceutical Firms
nodes.abstract:
Pharmaceutical firms talk about artificial intelligence more than almost any other industry, and the claims are large. Industry estimates suggest the AI-in-drug-development market is growing at over 30% annually (Grand View Research, 2023), and consulting analyses project that AI could compress discovery-to-proof-of-concept timelines by 35% to 50% (BCG & Wellcome, 2023). But such projections rest largely on company-reported figures that have yet to be independently verified (Nature, 2023). The reality is less settled. As of first quarter of 2026, no AI-discovered drug has received full FDA approval (Guldvog, 2026) and the most advanced candidate has only recently reported randomized Phase 2a results (Xu et al., 2025). AI-discovered molecules clear Phase I safety testing at unusually high rates, but their Phase II performance, the first real test of efficacy in patients, is not better than historical industry averages (Jayatunga et al., 2024). Separate literature shows that, despite many firms disclosing AI use, it may actually mean little. Because AI disclosure is voluntary, inexpensive, and difficult to verify, firms have incentives to overstate it. Barrios et al. (2025) show that AI disclosures predict operational performance only when backed by credible AI hiring, and Basnet et al. (2025) find markets reward concrete implementation claims but ignore speculative ones. Both studies measure success financially, through stock returns or firm performance. They suggest that AI disclosures fall into two kinds: substantive disclosures backed by actual implementation, and symbolic ones that are not. Whether that difference in AI disclosure predicts safety and regulatory outcomes has not been examined.
We therefore ask two questions. Does AI adoption by pharmaceutical firms change postmarket drug safety, measured by product recalls and adverse-event mortality, and regulatory performance, measured by approval activity and review times? And does any such effect depend on whether a firm's AI disclosure is substantive or symbolic?
We address these questions with a firm-year panel of publicly traded US pharmaceutical firms. The panel covers 2010 to 2024 and currently includes 323 firms and 4,845 firm-year observations. AI disclosure is extracted from SEC 10-K and 8-K filings through the EDGAR API, using a keyword dictionary based on Ferreira and Carneiro (2025). First, we classify each firm's AI disclosures as substantive or symbolic. Substantive disclosures describe a specific implemented application in discovery, clinical development, manufacturing, or pharmacovigilance. Symbolic disclosures are generic, forward-looking, or risk-factor boilerplate. Classification is LLM-assisted and validated against independent human coding of a stratified sample, with inter-rater agreement reported. Then, we tag the stage of AI use following the FDA/CDER lifecycle taxonomy: target identification, molecule design and preclinical work, clinical trials, manufacturing and quality, and postmarket safety.
Our outcome variables come from three public sources merged to the panel. Recall outcomes come from FDA Enforcement Reports (openFDA), covering 911 human drug recall events involving listed firms during the sample period. Mortality outcomes come from FAERS death reports linked to firms. Approval outcomes are drawn from Drugs@FDA: counts of NDA and BLA approvals per firm-year, submission-to-approval review times, and expedited-pathway designations. All outcomes are revenue-normalized.
Our preliminary evidence shows that AI-disclosing firms average 6.99 recalls per firm-year before disclosure, falling to 5.11 afterward, with declines in death reports as well, while non-disclosing firms show no comparable shift. We treat these patterns as descriptive rather than causal. Firms that disclose AI are larger and carry broader product portfolios. The number of firms observed also falls sharply as event time increases. And a firm's disclosure year tells us when it chose to talk about AI, not when it started using it. Reverse causality is also plausible: firms may adopt AI in quality or pharmacovigilance functions precisely because they experienced safety problems.
In the analysis process, we will estimate staggered difference-in-differences models centered on each firm's first AI disclosure year, with planned controls for firm size, R&D intensity, firm age, years since IPO, and therapeutic-area composition. The same design applies to regulatory outcomes in terms of approval counts and review time because AI adoption in discovery and clinical development should plausibly move regulatory throughput even where it does not move safety. The substantive-versus-symbolic classification enters the estimation directly. Rather than analyzing the two groups separately, we include both in a single model and allow the treatment effect to differ by disclosure type. This preserves the full panel, produces an event-study path for each group, and lets us test directly whether the difference between them is statistically significant. Symbolic disclosers face the same incentives to announce AI as substantive ones but have not implemented it, so they serve as a within-treatment comparison group rather than a second set of controls. If the safety improvements we observe reflect AI use, they should appear among substantive disclosers and be absent among symbolic ones. If instead both groups improve, the pattern more likely reflects the kind of firm that talks about AI than AI itself, and this is the result that would most change how we read the preliminary evidence.
The study aims to separate AI hype from AI readiness. Prior work has shown that AI disclosures predict financial performance only when firms actually invest in AI. We explore whether the same holds for drug safety and regulatory outcomes, where the stakes are patient harm rather than share price. The measurement pipeline is built entirely from public data and can be reused, which matters because no registry of AI-enabled drug development currently exists (Jayatunga et al., 2024). The findings will interest the FDA as it develops AI guidance, and the SEC as it looks more closely at AI claims in corporate filings.
References
Barrios, J. M., Campbell, J. L., Johnson, R. G., & Liu, Y. C. (2025). Artificially intelligent or artificially inflated? Determinants and informativeness of corporate AI disclosures. SSRN Electronic Journal.
Basnet, A., Elias, M., Salganik-Shoshan, G., Walker, T., & Zhao, Y. (2025). Analyzing the market's reaction to AI narratives in corporate filings. International Review of Financial Analysis, 105, 104378.
Boston Consulting Group & Wellcome. (2023). Unlocking the potential of AI in drug discovery. Wellcome Trust.

nodes.title: Automation or Augmentation? Common Knowledge Frictions and Auditor Pipeline Risk
nodes.affiliation: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics
nodes.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping skill-intensive professions, and the audit profession sits at the front of this transformation: major accounting firms are investing heavily in AI tools that can automate document retrieval, anomaly detection, and other junior audit tasks, while simultaneously asserting that AI complements human auditors and raises their productivity. Public narratives diverge sharply between these automation and augmentation views, and the academic evidence is equally split - some studies find AI displaces junior audit tasks and reduces headcount, while others find AI adoption raises demand for human auditors. Against this backdrop, the U.S. audit labor market displays a puzzling combination of facts. Accounting enrollments and CPA exam participation have declined steadily, shrinking the entry-level pipeline. Yet audit firms continue to post stable or growing numbers of junior vacancies, and positions take longer to fill. Standard theory predicts that falling supply against stable demand should push wages up, but auditor wages have barely moved across experience levels for over a decade. Each fact alone is easy to explain; the conjunction is not. A competitive market would bid the wage up until the smaller cohort cleared. Market power, wage norms, menu costs, and cobweb entry lags can each account for one fact, but none can generate declining entry, elevated vacancies, and flat wages together.
This paper proposes and tests one explanation: asymmetric common knowledge about AI's two effects. Everyone - students and firms alike - observes both the automation narrative (AI displaces junior tasks) and the augmentation narrative (AI makes each auditor more valuable). The friction is not disagreement about fundamentals but uncertainty about whether others have absorbed the same information. The automation story travels through public professional media and is close to common knowledge: everyone knows it, and knows that everyone knows it. The augmentation story propagates through decentralized, university-borne experience - courses, pilots, peer discussion - whose reach nobody can verify for anyone else.
We formalize this mechanism in a model in which students enter the qualified-auditor pipeline before firms recruit. Entry decisions reinforce each other: the benefits of joining a profession - specialized instruction, peer learning, firm training, employer recognition - depend on cohort scale, so each student's entry response to a technological effect is amplified by expected peer entry. Because augmentation sits further from common knowledge than automation, its positive effect receives less coordination amplification, and entry contracts even when the technology favors human-AI complementarity. After the cohort is fixed, firms simultaneously post wage scales. Wage posting is itself a coordination game: a firm that raises pay unilaterally mostly poaches applicants from rivals and invites matching, so each posted scale weights rivals' expected scales more than fundamentals. Each shock then passes into wages at its own commonality rate: the wage prices the common automation content, while the unpriced augmentation content accumulates as unfilled positions. The model's sharpest result is that this asymmetry is not merely sufficient but necessary: under any symmetric-information wage-setting friction, rising vacancies and flat junior offers are mutually exclusive, because both reflect the same composite of news. The joint pattern in the data therefore identifies the friction.
Higher-order beliefs cannot be measured at scale, so we test the mechanism through its equilibrium footprints and an exposure design. We use departures of AI faculty from U.S. universities to industry as shocks to the local formation of common knowledge about AI's augmentation value. Universities generate shared curricula, assignments, and seminars that let many students learn the same things and infer that their peers are learning them too; a departure weakens this shared signal without changing AI's technical capabilities, firms' production technology, or the widely publicized automation narrative. Using matched employer-employee data from Revelio Labs, job postings from Burning Glass, and audit outcomes from Audit Analytics, we estimate stacked difference-in-differences models around departure events, comparing treated universities and states with matched local controls and geographically neighboring never-treated states.
Four results line up with the model's predictions. First, entry falls: the share of accounting graduates entering audit careers drops by 2.5 percentage points, a 5.7% decline from baseline, emerging three years after a departure and peaking at six. Second, excess demand appears on both margins: junior auditor postings rise 17.4%, and postings remain open 4.8% longer, concentrated precisely at the junior level where the missing cohort would have arrived. Third, wages do not respond: staff and management auditor wages in treated states are statistically and economically indistinguishable from controls throughout the event window. Fourth, audit quality erodes with a long lag: abnormal accruals rise and modified opinions fall as smaller, less AI-complementary cohorts accumulate within offices.
The findings reframe the auditor pipeline problem. It is not simply automation displacing workers: no agent in our model, or plausibly in the data, is wrong about the technology. It is a coordination failure rooted in beliefs about others, and it identifies universities as upstream information infrastructure. Because universities generate the shared learning environment that makes augmentation knowledge common, they are uniquely positioned to repair the friction. The model also implies a firm-side lever: earlier, credible disclosure of pipeline statistics would rebuild common knowledge among firms and compress the vacancy-wage wedge. The mechanism generalizes to any skilled profession where a technology simultaneously automates routine tasks and augments human judgment, and where the two narratives travel through channels that differ in their distance from common knowledge.

nodes.title: Do Non-Competes Slow the Diffusion of AI?
nodes.abstract: We investigate whether noncompete agreements (NCAs) slow the diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI). Using state-level NCA events from 2009 to 2024 and individual employment histories from Revelio Labs, we find that stronger enforceability sharply reduces the AI labor mobility. Across firms, AI worker inflows and outflows fall by roughly 23 and 27 percent of their means, and the declines appear for both in-state and cross-state moves, pointing to a broad mobility friction rather than a narrow relocation channel. Downstream, stronger enforceability is followed by 16 to 21 percent fewer AI patent applications and fewer new AI-related firms. Because AI know-how is largely tacit and embodied in scarce human capital, restricting mobility appears to slow AI diffusion rather than merely redistribute its returns.

nodes.title: Start Wide, Not Deep: What a Cross-Functional First Cohort Teaches an Institution About Itself
nodes.abstract:
When a large organization starts with AI, the instinct is to go deep in one place: pick the department with the clearest use case, run a pilot, prove it, expand. It is an efficient way to learn a great deal about one department.

Cuyahoga Community College - Ohio's first and largest community college, roughly 3,000 faculty and staff across four campuses serving more than 42,000 students - went the other way. Between February and April 2026 it ran its first AI program with fifteen people drawn from fifteen different corners of the institution: faculty across nursing, IT, English and creative arts; deans; IT services; compliance and risk; interactive marketing; executive operations; the corporate training arm; and administrative staff. Each was already curious about AI in their own role. None were sent.

This case study makes the argument for that starting shape, shows what it produced, and is honest about what it did not.

**The core argument.** A first cohort's most valuable output is not the pilot result. It is what the institution learns about itself - which roles take to these tools, which workflows they actually land in, where the friction is real versus rhetorical, and who the credible internal voices turn out to be. A departmental pilot cannot produce that, because it only ever reports on one department. Going wide costs efficiency and buys institutional intelligence, and for an organization deciding how to spend the next three years, that trade is usually correct.

**What attendees will learn:**

1. **A selection logic built on representation and existing interest.** We will cover how the cohort was assembled - breadth across function, campus and seniority, weighted toward people already exploring AI in their own work - and why volunteer curiosity outperformed both mandated participation and technical aptitude as a selection criterion at this stage. The executive sponsor's stated goal was people open enough to explore, not people who already knew the most.

2. **Tailoring the learning to each participant's actual goals, and what that costs.** Rather than a common curriculum with a shared exercise, participants worked their own real problems throughout: a nursing instructor on personalized student feedback, a compliance director on preliminary risk research, an executive operations leader on reporting into a president's office, an IT faculty member on assessment design for a software automation course. We will be concrete about the delivery model that makes this possible - small cohort, in-person core sessions with a virtual option, follow-on 1:1 coaching sessions - and about where it is expensive and where it is fragile.

3. **Cross-pollination as a designed outcome, not a happy accident.** Faculty learning beside compliance, beside marketing, beside IT services produced a shared institutional vocabulary and a pattern of transfer across functions that a departmental cohort structurally forecloses. We will show specific examples of a technique or workflow moving between functions that had no prior reason to talk, and name the conditions that made it possible - including the ones that were uncomfortable.

4. **The executive sponsor as an embedded observer.** The college's CIO did not sponsor from a distance; she participated as a learner alongside her own staff and faculty. That put a senior leader in the room watching, in real time, how fifteen different roles engaged with the same tools and applied them to genuinely different work. We will argue this is one of the most underrated returns on a first cohort - leadership intelligence that no readout, dashboard or vendor report reproduces - and show how it shaped the institution's subsequent planning.

5. **What we measured, and what we would measure differently.** Beyond hours saved (a mean of 8.8 self-reported hours weekly), we tracked *capacity unlock* - 77% agreed AI freed them for important work they previously had no time for - and *new capability*, where 69% reported reaching a quality level they could not before. We also found what we now consider the healthiest governance signal available: concerns training should resolve did (the knowledge gap fell from five participants to zero, plagiarism from eleven to five, misinformation from nine to four), while concerns that should persist for any AI-using professional remained (data privacy held at eleven, accuracy at eleven, overdependence at ten). Participants ended more able to identify AI risk, not less worried about it.

**Honest limits.** Findings draw on a pre-program readiness survey (n=15), a post-program impact survey (n=13, 87% response), twelve matched pairs, and structured retrospectives with the executive sponsor after each phase. Self-reported time savings are self-reported. This cohort was intentionally curated and a second will not resemble it. Our recommendation measure used a 1-5 scale and is not a true NPS. We have no long-horizon follow-up yet showing whether gains held. We will also cover what emerged that we did not design for - including a backlog of unfinished cross-institutional workflows, and early signs that some participants may become credible peer teachers, which was never the program's premise and would require its own design.

**Approach and format.** Roughly two-thirds narrative case, one-third transferable framework, built for a room holding both practitioners deciding what to fund and researchers deciding what to study. The session will incorporate the client's voice through recorded participant and executive-sponsor segments; if scheduling permits, a member of the college's cohort will co-present live, and we will confirm with the program committee as the agenda firms.

**Who this is for.** Leaders responsible for enterprise AI enablement, HR and L&D teams designing internal upskilling, higher-education and executive-education administrators, and researchers studying AI adoption and organizational change. The setting is higher education; the constraints - distributed workforce, no discretionary time, high governance sensitivity, no appetite for a big-bang rollout - are not.

nodes.title: Human Interactions with Generative AI in Customer Service
nodes.abstract:
Implementing Generative AI technology within product offerings and business workflows has become a priority for many businesses. Leveraging tools like Microsoft Copilot and building agentic AI solutions drives conversations about productivity, efficiency, and elevated user experiences. As businesses work to offer products driven by Generative AI, this project asks how well the technology performs for native and non-native speakers of English. Essentially: do preferences from the model or the human influence the end interaction?

Model preference is defined in this project as models performing better on mainstream or standard American English due to unbalanced training data during model development. Human preference is defined in this project as differences in perceptions of AI conversational partners in comparison to human conversational partners. Preferences include perceptions or judgments related to the conversational partner's personality, trustworthiness, credibility, usefulness, etc.

This project specifically focuses on speech recognition models and voice-enabled agents in a customer service context with the goal of answering two research questions:
RQ1: How well do ASR models perform as AI transcription tools on customer service calls? Does the call center location impact transcription accuracy when one call center is non-US based? 
RQ2: Is a customer service agent perceived differently in terms of competence and dependability, human-likeness, and communicative flexibility depending on whether the listener thinks the agent is AI or a human? Does agent misunderstanding of the customer influence these perceptions? Does being an L1 or L2 English-speaking listener influence these perceptions?

This poster will detail the proposed methods of ongoing dissertation work. Critically, the methods provide a foundation for discussing ways of evaluating current and forward-looking generative AI solutions in a real world context. Questions around how to safely implement and monitor generative AI solutions go beyond traditional computer science methods. In this work specifically, language is the primary interaction of study.

First, automated speech recognition (ASR) models will be tested as transcription tools for customer service data. ASR models will generate transcripts for actual customer service calls from a Fortune 100 insurance company. Transcripts will be analyzed according to word error rate (WER) for calls where the call centers (and subsequently the agents) are US-based and where the agents are Phillipines-based. Results from these methods will answer RQ1. 

Secondly, native and non-native speakers of English will participate in a Matched Guise Task where they will hear a set of customer service calls. Call content will be similar to conversations found in the dataset for Experiment 1. All participants will hear the same set of dialogues. Each dialogue will randomly be assigned to be a conversation including an AI customer service agent, a human customer service agent, or undefined. This per-dialogue information will be randomized for each participant. Participants will then be asked to rate the customer service agent according to 7-point Likert scale ratings for polar elements such as "trustworthy-untrustworthy" or statements such as "I would trust this agent". The goal of this experiment is to see how ratings shift based on if the participant thinks they are listening to an AI agent or a human agent and if those perceptions are influenced by the participant being a native or non-native speaker of English. Results gathered using these methods will answer RQ2.

Both studies aim to showcase nuances in human-AI interactions from the perspective of ASR model and native and non-native English speaker preferences. As these technologies become more easily adoptable by companies, this work contributes to understanding human-AI interaction dynamics from native and non-native English speaker perspectives. Experiment one directly questions preferences within the model that can impact transcript accuracy. Experiment two questions perceptions of customer service agent performance based on if the agent is human or AI and whether the judge is a native or non-native English speaker.

nodes.title: Governing Knowledge Across Humans and Machines: How AI Reshapes Organizational Knowledge Management Through Externally Specified and Internally Learned Representations
nodes.abstract:
Alongside the relentless scaling of models, data, and computing infrastructure, another defining trend in enterprise AI is the integration of generative models with other knowledge resources. AI capabilities are increasingly realized through hybrid configurations, such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), AI agents that invoke conventional deterministic software, and human-in-the-loop arrangements that retain human judgement and authority. These configurations seek to harness the power of generative AI while improving its reliability and trustworthiness through grounded information, deterministic execution, and human oversight.

Yet existing research on organizational knowledge management lacks a coherent account of what fundamentally differentiates knowledge resources and how they can complement one another in hybrid configurations. Without such an account, hybrid AI innovations are difficult to interpret cumulatively: each appears as an isolated technical advancement rather than an application of more general design principles; moreover, how organizations should design, manage, and govern these configurations remains underdeveloped.

To address this gap, we develop a theoretical framework drawing on research on organizational cognition, knowledge structures, and tacit knowledge, informed by recent advances in neural networks and large language models (LLMs). Specifically, we posit that the distinction between explicit knowledge and tacit skill reflects a fundamental difference in how knowledge is represented: explicit knowledge is encoded and communicated using pre-existing codes, languages, or other representational schemes. For example, a procedure written in natural language uses an established language that others can interpret, use, and share. Tacit skills, by contrast, are acquired through practice, feedback, and repeated experience with task environments. Through this process, the internal representation encoding the skill is itself learned rather than specified using a pre-existing representational scheme. Because this representation emerges through experience rather than deliberate specification, it is not directly observable-even to the person possessing the skill-and the underlying knowledge can be difficult to articulate fully. Tacit skill therefore cannot be fully passed on using shared codes or languages; others must develop their own internal representations experientially.

Traditionally, machines have operated primarily with externally specified representations: their rules, procedures, and task knowledge are encoded in programming languages or computer codes. Advances in neural networks and LLMs have created a machine analogue to human tacit skill acquisition: machines can develop capabilities resembling human tacit skills through internally learned representations formed in large-scale training. This yields a two-by-two framework: knowledge may be acquired and applied by humans or machines, and its representation may be externally specified or internally learned. The framework identifies four modes of organizational knowledge management with distinct strengths, limitations, and implications for how knowledge can be combined and governed.

Our framework reveals implications for how organizational knowledge can be replicated, combined, and governed as organizations seek to scale AI. First, internally learned representations allow machines to acquire capabilities resembling human tacit skills that are difficult or infeasible to reproduce through explicit programming because their fine-grained knowledge cannot be fully articulated using existing codes or languages. Large-scale training instead allows these inarticulable nuances to become encoded in internal representations. However, unlike human tacit skills, which must be developed experientially by each individual, the resulting machine representations can be easily copied and deployed at scale. Internally learned machine knowledge thus combines the acquisition logic of tacit skill with the replicability of explicit knowledge.

Moreover, different knowledge modes can complement and scaffold one another. RAG complements powerful but sometimes unreliable tacit-like capabilities by grounding their application in externally maintained data, while tool use (i.e., allowing AI agents to invoke conventional deterministic software) delegates tasks requiring precision and deterministic execution to software whose rules and procedures must be explicitly specified and coded by humans. These configurations illustrate a broader design principle: limitations of one knowledge mode can be managed by coupling it with the strengths of another.

More fundamentally, AI opens new pathways through which knowledge represented in one mode can guide action in another. Making articulated human knowledge machine-operable historically required labor-intensive recoding by programmers into formal code. Emerging approaches such as Agent Skills now allow explicit knowledge expressed in natural language to directly guide machine action without this recoding step. This both lowers the barrier to articulating task knowledge for machine use and makes previously human-oriented stores of organizational knowledge-such as procedures, policies, manuals, and playbooks-directly operable by machines, potentially unlocking substantial value from knowledge that organizations have already articulated.

Finally, our analysis reframes AI governance around trade-offs among knowledge modes and the pathways connecting them. Externally specified representations are more inspectable, revisable, and controllable, but can be costly or infeasible when knowledge resists articulation; internally learned representations can capture tacit-like nuances but are much less observable and harder to validate and control. Hybrid configurations manage these trade-offs by grounding, constraining, or scaffolding one mode with another. As AI opens more pathways through which knowledge becomes machine-operable, organizations must govern which knowledge artifacts are authorized to guide machine action, how modes are combined, and how outputs are validated before becoming socially actionable.

In conclusion, advances in neural networks and LLMs reveal a machine analogue to human tacit skill acquisition and thereby expose a fundamental representational distinction across the human-machine boundary. Our framework shows how AI unbundles properties of knowledge that organizational theory has historically treated as linked: internally learned machine capabilities retain tacit-like acquisition and opacity yet become readily replicable. This creates an asymmetry: organizations can replicate and deploy tacit-like machine capabilities far faster than they can verify their reliability, making scalability itself a source of governance risk. Organizations have always combined heterogeneous knowledge modes, but AI greatly expands the pathways through which they can be coupled, creating new capabilities alongside new risks and bottlenecks. Scaling AI is therefore fundamentally a knowledge-governance problem: organizations must govern hybrid cognition by configuring how human and machine knowledge modes interact so their complementary strengths can be harnessed reliably and responsibly.

nodes.title: When GAI Writes: Generative AI Disclosure and Analyst Forecasts
nodes.abstract:
Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) is reshaping the world since ChatGPT was released available to the public on November 30, 2022. Recent evidence also shows GAI produces a detectable share of new text in disclosures, for example, financial reporting (Blankespoor et al., 2025). However, there is limited evidence on its impact on financial markets (Cao et al, 2026). As corporate disclosures rarely travel directly from firms to prices, they pass first through a layer of professional intermediaries whose business is to process them. Sell-side analysts read firms' filings, press releases, and conference call remarks, and transform them into the forecasts that anchor market expectations.

Therefore, we examine how the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) in financial reporting affects the behaviors of sell-side financial analysts. Using report-level measures of GAI usage from Blankespoor et al. (2026), we identify likely GAI users based on the standardized change in GAI usage around the release of ChatGPT. Specifically, for each firm, we compute the difference between post-ChatGPT and pre-ChatGPT GAI usage in MD&A, scaled by the cross-sectional standard deviation of GAI usage. Firms with larger standardized increases are more likely to have adopted GAI. We validate this classification by showing that likely GENAI users experience a significant increase in GENAI usage in their financial reporting after the launch of ChatGPT. Then we examine the difference between likely GAI users and non- likely GAI users on analyst forecast behaviors around ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, mainly one-quarter-ahead forecasts. The results show that GAI usage in financial reporting writing is associated with better, not worse, forecast outcomes. Analyst's earnings forecast errors are smaller for likely GAI users after the release of ChatGPT, and forecast dispersion is lower. Additionally, the forecast consensus and analyst coverage are higher for likely GAI users. We find no evidence of reduced analyst effort, proxied by forecast revision activity. Taken together, our findings are inconsistent with the concern that machine-written disclosure has impaired the professional processing of firm information.

In the further analysis, we explore whether there is any difference in linguistic characteristics between the GAI users and non-likely GAI users, which might drive the results. We find that filings with higher GAI usage are more positive, shorter, and more specific. The results are consistent with Blankespoor et al. (2026), who use within-report analyses to contrast the linguistic properties of content that is the least versus most likely to use GAI and find that GAI content of MD&A tends to be more positively toned, more readable, and more specific. The above results lend support to our underlying mechanisms, as readability and specificity reduce analysts' processing costs (Lehavy et al., 2022; Hope et al., 2016) and positive sentiment is associated with positive forecasts. 

Additionally, we find that the relationship is more prominent for firms with lower risk proxied by lower leverage in fiscal year 2021, and firms with more analysts following in year 2021. We conclude with a battery of robustness tests that corroborate our findings. We re-estimate our main specification using alternative cutoffs for classifying likely GAI users, a shorter sample window that begins in 2008, clustering standard errors at the firm level, and re-estimate the results using annual forecast sample. These inferences are consistent with our main findings. 

We contribute to the literature on information processing by providing early evidence on how the automation of disclosure production affects the output of professional information intermediaries. A growing literature examines how analysts and investors use AI to consume information (Bradshaw et al. 2025; Christ et al. 2025; Cheng et al. 2025; Bertomeu et al. 2025; Kim, Muhn, and Nikolaev 2024). We ask the complementary, supply-side question: what happens to forecast quality when the documents analysts process are themselves machine-written? We thereby answer a question explicitly posed by Blankespoor et al. (2025), who document GAI usage but leave its consequences for information processing open. We also complement concurrent work relating AI-like disclosure language to market outcomes, e.g. aggregate trading outcomes and investor reactions (Irons 2024; Plate et al., 2024) by opening the intermediation channel through which such aggregate effects arise. Our evidence suggests one reason markets appear to have absorbed machine-written disclosure without disruption: the professionals who stand between firms and investors process it efficiently. To sum up, our findings suggest that concerns about generative AI degrading the quality of corporate disclosure may be overstated, and inform ongoing regulatory discussions about whether firms' use of AI in financial reporting warrants disclosure or oversight.

nodes.title: Too Neat to Be True? AI-Generated Review Summary Discrepancies and Consumer Response
nodes.abstract:
Research Motivation
Online reviews affect sales (Chevalier and Mayzlin, 2006), and generative AI is rapidly becoming part of the interface through which consumers encounter them. Platforms increasingly use large language models to interpret those reviews and present their own condensed assessments. AI-generated summaries (AIGS) are meant to help consumers understand a large and heterogeneous review record. Existing work treats the AIGS, once introduced, as given (Kim et al., 2024; Su et al., 2024). Its discrepancy from the contemporaneous review record has received little attention.
The convenience of this summarization layer, however, creates a new information problem. An AIGS may not agree with the human reviews displayed alongside it. An average rating stands in a transparent relationship to the ratings beneath it. An AIGS is produced through an opaque process of selecting, weighting, and compressing review content. It may emphasize unrepresentative opinions or remain anchored in an earlier review record as new reviews accumulate. When the two sources conflict, consumers must determine which one better represents the service. AIGS-review discrepancy therefore bears on trust and purchase decisions.
The consequences of such disagreement differ by direction and by attribute. An AIGS that is more favorable than recent human reviews may appear overly promotional or misleading. One that is less favorable may be interpreted as cautious or conservative. Hotel attributes also differ substantially in their pre-purchase verifiability, consistent with the search-experience distinction (Nelson, 1970, 1974; Huang et al., 2009). A prospective guest can compare a claim about location with maps and transit times before booking. Service, cleanliness, and noise are learned primarily through the stay itself. Disagreement may therefore be more salient for attributes a guest can check in advance. We ask how the magnitude, direction, and attribute of a discrepancy relate to hotel demand.
Data and Methodology
We monitored Tripadvisor hotel pages in 31 major tourist and business cities in North America, Europe, and Asia over 2025, observing three waves of updates. The update interval rarely falls below two months, so we treat each two-month window with an unchanged AIGS as one period. This yielded 11,220 hotel-period observations for 4,389 hotels and review histories of 1,536,730 human reviews.
To place the two texts on a common scale, we label both with a single large language model procedure. Instructions, prompts, and parsing rules are held fixed across the corpus. For each text, the procedure identifies references to eight hotel attributes (location, atmosphere, rooms, value, noise, cleanliness, service, and amenities) and to overall emotional tone. Each mentioned item receives a score from 0 to 10; unmentioned items remain missing. The signed discrepancy is the AIGS score minus the median score among human reviews posted in the preceding 30 days. Its mean across non-missing dimensions gives the hotel-period discrepancy, whose absolute value is our main explanatory variable.
Purchase intent is not directly observable, so we impute demand from review counts in review-equivalent units. Reviews observed in period t are generated by demand in period t and in earlier periods. The review series is therefore a distributed lag of latent demand, and inverting this system recovers demand. The lag, calibrated from Tripadvisor view-to-booking and auxiliary Expedia booking-to-review data, places 68.5% of eventual reviews in the period of the initial view. We regress imputed demand on the absolute discrepancy with hotel fixed effects, add period fixed effects, and estimate direction-specific slopes, clustering by hotel. These specifications use 8,619 hotel-periods from 3,230 hotels. Each attribute is estimated separately.
Findings
Discrepancy magnitude is negatively associated with contemporaneous imputed demand within hotels (−0.964). The pattern remains when period fixed effects enter the specification (−1.002; both p < 0.01). The direction-specific estimates sharpen the result. The negative association is concentrated in periods of overstatement, in which the AIGS portrays the hotel more favorably than recent human reviews (−1.280, p < 0.01). Understatement does not lower imputed demand. The direction of a discrepancy therefore carries information that its magnitude alone leaves out.
Attribute by attribute, the overstatement slope is negative for seven of the eight hotel attributes and statistically significant for all seven. The ordering follows pre-purchase verifiability. Location carries the largest estimate (−1.432). Atmosphere (−1.338) and amenities (−1.264), which a listing and its photographs verify in part, follow. Rooms, service, cleanliness, and value come next at smaller magnitudes (−0.909 to −0.656). Noise does not exhibit the same pattern.
Implications
For research on platform information design, these results turn a feature usually treated as fixed into a variable. The discrepancy between an AIGS and the record beneath it varies within a property over time and is associated with imputed demand. The search-experience distinction was developed for product categories. It is informative at the attribute level inside one service category, where location and service occupy different points of one spectrum on a single page.
A platform can compute the discrepancy from material it already holds, namely the summary text and the review record. This comparison can therefore run continuously. A monitoring series records a discrepancy's magnitude, direction, and attributes. For a hotel, the AIGS belongs to a storefront the platform composes, and the attribute breakdown shows where a discrepancy concentrates. Tracing the feedback among summaries, bookings, and later reviews is the natural next step.
References
Chevalier, J.A. and Mayzlin, D. (2006) 'The effect of word of mouth on sales: online book reviews', Journal of Marketing Research, 43(3), pp. 345-354.
Huang, P., Lurie, N.H. and Mitra, S. (2009) 'Searching for experience on the web: an empirical examination of consumer behavior for search and experience goods', Journal of Marketing, 73(2), pp. 55-69.
Kim, A., Lu, Y., Ma, T. and Tan, Y. (2024) 'Less is more? Impact of AI-generated summaries on user engagement of video-sharing platforms'. Available at SSRN 5020305.
Nelson, P. (1970) 'Information and consumer behavior', Journal of Political Economy, 78(2), pp. 311-329.
Nelson, P. (1974) 'Advertising as information', Journal of Political Economy, 82(4), pp. 729-754.
Su, Y., Wang, Q., Qiu, L. and Chen, R. (2024) 'Navigating the sea of reviews: unveiling the effects of introducing AI-generated summaries in e-commerce'. Available at SSRN 4872205.

nodes.title: AI Scales-but Can It Deliver in High-Stakes Finance?
nodes.abstract:
The question financial institutions face when they scale AI 

AI has diffused rapidly through financial institutions. In a 2026 survey of 628 organizations across 151 jurisdictions, 81% reported AI adoption and 40% reported advanced adoption. Yet 55% of respondents-and 76% of large institutions-struggled to measure deployment value (Cambridge CCAF, 2026). The gap reflects a deeper distinction: output is easier to count than reliable delivery. Financial workflows bundle routine production with judgment-intensive verification. AI can scale routine production, but judgment determines whether its output becomes decision-ready. When verification remains the bottleneck, faster intermediate work need not shorten delivery. End-to-end productivity is therefore decision-ready work per unit of expert time at fixed assurance-not intermediate output. The question is whether AI improves that outcome after human judgment and verification. 

Existing evidence rarely answers this question. Firm-level studies infer aggregate effects without isolating routine from judgment-intensive work. Field experiments observe task output but mostly on bounded tasks-writing, support, coding, and consulting-where errors do not expose professionals to a live decision's full consequences. Such studies show whether AI accelerates a task, not whether it reduces the expert effort required to deliver the workflow. 

Standard AI evaluation datasets are further from production: exam questions are self-contained and scored against documented answers; real cases require deciding what evidence matters, what to rule out, and what risk remains. We call work high-stakes when error can cause substantial downstream harm and an identifiable person or firm remains professionally or legally accountable. That accountability cannot be delegated: any model output entering the decision must be reviewed by the human who answers for the outcome. 

A rare view into a high-stakes financial workflow 

Evidence from high-stakes work is usually out of reach: real inputs paired with expert judgments are confidential. Cryptocurrency offers a rare exception. In decentralized finance (DeFi), smart contracts - code that automatically holds and moves users' crypto assets - replace traditional financial intermediaries. Before such code goes live, professional auditors read it and report flaws. Both the code and the paid audit reports are unusually public. Our data link code and reports for roughly 8,000 DeFi projects in a market that has held 200 billion dollars and lost 7.6 billions to documented attacks.

The setting combines three rarely observed features. First, it is genuinely high-stakes: the protocol team decides whether to deploy, and the audit firm attaches its name to disclosed findings. Credible assurance combines routine code inspection with judgment about protocol economics and plausible attack paths. Second, for each protocol, we observe code the auditor reviewed and findings a paid firm published. Reports are professional judgments, not infallible ground truth. Our primary test is report-relative recall: whether AI recovers disclosed findings. We label model-only findings as report-relative false positives for benchmarking; because reports may omit genuine findings, that label denotes disagreement, not necessarily factual error. Third, standardized model evaluations across thousands of matched protocols reveal benchmark-relative misses, additional flags, and performance variation. 

Framework: why reliability thresholds-not average accuracy-govern adoption 

We model AI assistance where a human remains accountable for the final judgment. The primary empirical constraint is report-relative false negatives-disclosed findings the model fails to recover. Many such misses mean the model does not reproduce the professional benchmark; when a missed finding is genuine, deployed funds may face difficult-to-reverse losses. Model-only flags create a secondary cost because each requires adjudication, although some may be genuine auditor omissions. 

The economic question is whether AI improves the whole workflow, not whether it generates useful output. High report-relative miss rates do not justify reducing independent checking; excessive additional flags increase the verification burden. Reliability cannot be reduced to average accuracy: the primary requirement is a sufficiently low miss rate, especially on severe cases; the secondary requirement is manageable additional-flag volume. Because we do not observe expert time directly, these error profiles identify necessary-but not sufficient-conditions for labor savings; they do not measure productivity. 

Findings 

Against this standard, none of the frontier models we evaluate-GPT-5.5, Claude Fable, or Gemini 3.5 Pro-meets the reliability conditions required for end-to-end productivity. More strikingly, even the best-performing configuration recovers only 59% of disclosed findings and 41% of severe findings, with no model satisfying both reliability thresholds. Scaffolding, retrieval, and multi-pass review improve recall by no more than 10 percentage points. This does not mean LLMs add no value: reasoning models identify contextual findings beyond predefined rules or pattern matching. But outperforming conventional automation does not clear the reliability bar. A model can matter without being dependable enough for accountable work. 

To locate the shortfall, we compare model and auditor findings by vulnerability type, severity, protocol complexity, and pattern frequency. Two patterns emerge. First, report-relative misses concentrate in attack types infrequent in our sample, so average performance conceals long-tail shortfalls where reliable coverage matters most. Second, performance declines with reasoning depth: models handle familiar patterns more reliably but struggle with multi-step, counterfactual reasoning about interactions between code and economic incentives. Higher capability does not eliminate this gap. The binding weakness is uneven reliability on long-tail, reasoning-intensive cases where professional judgment is hardest to substitute. 

The division of labor is therefore specific. AI's most plausible near-term role is the mechanical layer-screening known vulnerability patterns, checking standards, and triaging code. Human auditors retain economic judgment: interpreting incentives, tracing novel attacks, and adjudicating flags; accountable protocol decision-makers own deployment. AI can scale expert assistance before it can scale accountable delivery. 

Contribution and fit with "AI Innovation at Scale" 

To our knowledge, this is the first task-level evidence on AI in a high-stakes financial workflow, measuring benchmark-relative reliability against observed professional judgments rather than adoption proxies or generic benchmarks. Our portable design pairs observable inputs with disclosed professional outputs and maps report-relative misses and additional flags into necessary-but not sufficient-conditions for labor savings. Scaling routine production is not end-to-end delivery: the models we test do not yet meet the reliability conditions required for an accountable human to do less without sacrificing assurance.

nodes.title: AI Human Capital, Real Outcomes, and Management Forecast Accuracy: Evidence from Clinical Trials
nodes.abstract:
Motivation. 
Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely heralded as transformative, yet its returns are strikingly uneven: one recent report finds that 95 percent of organizations see no return on their in-house AI investment. This unevenness raises two questions of first-order importance to managers and investors: when does AI create value, and through which workers? We address these questions in the pharmaceutical industry, where AI is increasingly deployed across the drug-development process and where clinical trials generate granular, verifiable, project-level records of a firm's core operating activity. Clinical trials are also a unique setting to study disclosure and forecast quality: sponsors must register an expected completion date and update it over the trial's life, producing a mandatory, verifiable, non-financial management forecast that is ultimately settled against a realized date.

Data and methodology. 
We measure AI human capital at the worker level using online professional-profile data from Revelio Labs, classifying positions as AI-related and, crucially, distinguishing AI-skilled professionals with pharmaceutical domain expertise (clinical and research roles, and data scientists holding a life-science degree) from those with a primarily technical, computer-science or infrastructure background. We link these measures to roughly 12,000 interventional trials sponsored by 392 U.S.-listed pharmaceutical firms over 2010-2022, drawn from ClinicalTrials.gov. Because AI staffing is not randomly assigned, we identify its effects from variation within a firm's own workforce: all models include firm fixed effects and phase-by-disease-by-year fixed effects, and we complement this design with entropy balancing and a leads-and-lags falsification test. We study three trial-level outcomes that together reveal whether, and how, AI creates value: (i) trial completion, a verifiable operating milestone; (ii) the stock-market reaction to the completion announcement, which captures investors' revised valuation of the firm; and (iii) the accuracy of the firm's completion-date forecast, which captures its ability to plan and deliver the trial on schedule.

Findings. 
First, AI human capital raises the probability that a trial is completed; a one-standard-deviation increase raises completion by about 4.4 percent, identified entirely within firm. This effect is delivered by domain experts: the per-standard-deviation effect for domain workers (about 3.4 percent) is roughly double that for non-domain technical workers (about 1.6 percent), and it is concentrated among senior domain staff. Examining the mechanism, AI reduces terminations for strategic and safety reasons (avoidable failures) but not terminations for lack of efficacy, indicating that AI helps firms run and triage trials more effectively rather than making drugs work. Second, the market prices these completions: a one-standard-deviation increase in AI is associated with a completion abnormal return about 33 basis points higher, and this reaction concentrates in firms with a less transparent information environment (low analyst coverage, high illiquidity), where completions are most informative. The reaction is more pronounced for firms richer in domain experts (over 38 basis points), reinforcing the value of integrating AI skills with domain knowledge. Third, AI does not improve completion-forecast accuracy on average, but it sharply improves it where forecasting is hard: among the most analytically complex trials, a one-standard-deviation increase in AI reduces the delay between the promised and realized completion date by about 2.4 months and cuts the probability of a twelve-month-plus slip by roughly a third. Decomposing the forecast miss into the promised horizon and the realized duration shows that high-AI firms finish complex trials sooner, shortening realized duration about twice as much as they shorten their promises, so more accurate forecasts arise from more efficient execution rather than from more conservative reporting.

Implications. 
The returns to AI are context-specific and depend on who inside the firm does the work: value resides in experienced, domain-expert employees rather than in generic technical headcount. For managers and investors, realizing AI's potential in complex, knowledge-intensive settings therefore requires pairing AI capability with deep domain expertise. The study contributes to (i) the economics of AI and firm productivity, by providing direct, project-level evidence of AI's operating effects and identifying domain expertise as the key complement; (ii) the accounting literature using clinical trials, by linking AI human capital to trial completion and to the accuracy of mandatory management forecasts; and (iii) research on management-forecast quality and real decisions, by exploiting a setting in which promised and realized outcomes are both observed to show that AI improves forecasts by changing operations, not reporting.

nodes.title: Order to Cash Without Adding Headcount: What Actually Ships When a Mid-Market Distributor Puts AI Into Operations
nodes.abstract:
Mid-market distributors and e-commerce operators rarely fail at AI because the models are weak. They fail at the seam between a model and an operation that already runs. A pilot is scoped by a vendor, it demos well against clean data, and then it meets a real order path where the quote, the pick, the invoice, the shipment and the ledger entry are held together by people who improvise. Nobody owns that seam, so the pilot is quietly abandoned and the company concludes AI is not ready.

This session describes an operating model built from the inside of companies in the five to fifty million dollar revenue band, run by a practitioner who owns the production systems rather than advising on them. The method is narrow on purpose. Find the leak, which is the one step in the order to cash path where work is redone, delayed or re-keyed. Build a system for that step alone and put it into production behind the process that already exists. Hold it, meaning someone is accountable for it on the days it degrades. Then repeat, instead of buying a platform that promises the whole path at once.

The talk works through where this holds and where it does not, using the operational surfaces that carry real volume in distribution and e-commerce: warehouse and inventory movement, invoicing, shipping documentation, bookkeeping reconciliation and the CRM record that everything else keys off. It covers what changes in the operating model itself: how work gets specified when the builder is also the operator, what governance looks like without an internal data team, why the retirement decision matters more than the launch decision, and how to tell within weeks whether a deployment is earning or being carried.

The session is aimed at practitioners deciding where to place a first or second AI system, and at researchers studying adoption in firms too small to staff an AI function and too large to run the process by hand. It offers a candid account of what survives contact with an operation and what does not, including deployments that were shut down after they were measured.

nodes.title: AI Automation and Effort Allocation: Evidence from Sophisticated Investors
nodes.abstract:
In the asset management industry, too much focus has been placed on the direct investment implications of AI. In this solo-authored paper, "AI Automation and Effort Allocation: Evidence from Sophisticated Investors," I ask a related but different question: how do investors make complementary use of AI? Specifically, I examine how AI complements fund managers via its labor-saving capacity. I show that not all (fundamental) hedge funds adopt AI, but for those that do, they increase earnings call participation (with more call appearances and more questions on an average call) after AI adoption.
Artificial intelligence can do more than automate work: it can redirect skilled workers toward the tasks where human judgment matters most. My research asks whether, in the AI era, high-skilled workers devote more effort to human-intensive tasks, and I study this question in the hedge fund industry. Hedge funds are sophisticated investors who manage clients' money by developing informational advantages. They build these advantages by gathering information from two main sources: digital corporate filings and earnings conference calls. The difference is important: conference calls require real-time human interaction, while corporate filings do not.
Before adopting AI, it was extraordinarily difficult for humans to download and process the enormous volume of corporate filings in a timely way. AI makes that task feasible and performs it much more effectively. I show that when hedge funds adopt AI to automatically handle corporate filings, they reallocate time and effort toward earnings call participation. After adopting AI, hedge funds attend more earnings calls and ask more questions. In other words, AI shifts effort across information-acquisition tasks rather than simply replacing labor.
This shift has important consequences. I show hedge funds that adopt AI and then participate in earnings calls make better investment decisions, executing more profitable stock trades and achieving higher returns. The broader message of this research is that the power of AI lies not only in substitution, but also in redirection. We often focus on automation's disruptive side, such as robots replacing delivery workers. But that is only part of the story. My research proposes and tests a different view of the human-machine relationship: AI does not just replace human effort; it also increases effort in non-AI tasks that humans do best.
The central insight of my study is that AI frees up human effort for hedge funds to focus more on information acquisition activities that require human interactions. I combine two unique datasets to investigate my hypothesis. First, I identify each hedge fund's participation in the universe of virtual and in-person US conference calls over 2006-2017. Second, I use IP addresses and their retrieval speed and volume in SEC EDGAR log files to identify which funds adopt AI to automate the collection of machine-based information. Third, I document that this shift in information acquisition effort translates into better investment performance-hedge funds' post-automation call participation is associated with greater stock trade performance.
I examine two core empirical relations: the automation-participation relation, where left-hand-side earnings call participation is regressed on right-hand-side AI adoption (in the previous quarter/year); and the participation-performance relation where I explore the stock trade performance effect of post-automation earnings call participation. To this end, I hypothesize that hedge funds tend to increase earnings call participation following AI adoption in the first participation hypothesis, and that hedge funds will achieve better investment performance by extracting value-relevant information from earnings calls after automating SEC downloading in the second performance hypothesis.
To examine the first participation hypothesis, I first use a dynamic difference-in-differences empirical setup to provide descriptive evidence on hedge funds' earnings call participation behavior around AI adoption as a baseline. Additionally, I find stronger participation effects for larger, older, lower-portfolio-turnover funds, consistent with larger funds being more flexible with human capital redeployment, older funds being more informationally advantaged, and lower-portfolio-turnover funds relying more on a fundamental-investing approach. To further corroborate the causal interpretation of the automation-participation relation, I use a technology salience instrument to pin down a causal relation between AI adoption and earnings call participation. The basic idea is to use fundamental hedge funds' technology salience induced by local quants' initial 13-F filings to instrument for their AI adoption decisions. The IV test results confirm the positive and significant automation-participation relation in the baseline and indicate that the relation is likely causal.
To examine the second performance hypothesis, I construct a long-short portfolio that consists of stocks purchased minus sold by post-automation call participating HFs. The positive return spread speaks to profitable trades associated with post-automation call participation, consistent with human-interaction-based information extracted from earnings calls being value-relevant. I further find that the trade performance effect is concentrated in hard-to-research stocks, consistent with the marginal benefit of information acquisition being largest for informationally opaque stocks.
My empirical findings have implications for revisiting the productivity effects of automation technologies in the task-based framework. Prior studies focus on either new task creation or existing task substitution. In the former case, automation creates new tasks that require human effort, reflecting pure task complementarity, whereas in the latter case automation replaces human effort at some existing tasks, reflecting pure task substitution. 
What is missing in the empirical literature is a third case that lies between the two extremes, where task complementarity is embedded in existing task substitution. To shed light on this gap, I empirically identify a novel effort-reallocation mechanism through which automation raises productivity for high-skilled workers performing partially automatable tasks. The empirical effort-reallocation channel in my study also echoes the theory evidence on the time allocation mechanism in a contemporaneous paper by Gans and Goldfarb (2026), where the authors extend a classic production model with the case in which machines replace tasks of a given quality, and time is reallocated across the remaining manual tasks.
Another major twist in this paper is exhibited in contrast to the common replacement narrative associated with robotics automation: I show that AI automation does not just replace human effort, it also increases the amount of effort that high-skilled knowledge workers devote to human-centered tasks.

nodes.title: Racing or Partnering? Adoption Timing and Collaboration Strategies of Generative AI in the Creator Markets
nodes.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is transforming creator markets, yet little is known about how creators should use it once the technology becomes widely accessible. Prior research has largely asked whether firms or individuals should employ GenAI by comparing AI-generated and human-generated output. As GenAI becomes embedded in organizational workflows and individual practice, however, the more consequential question is when to adopt and how much of the creative process to delegate. Drawing on diffusion of innovation theory, we extend diffusion thinking to two-sided creator markets and argue that adoption timing shapes the content value available from a maturing technological and normative environment, whereas collaboration mode shapes how much of that value audiences attribute to the human creator. Using data from Wattpad, we find that later GenAI adoption is associated with higher audience engagement, whereas more AI-dominant collaboration is associated with lower engagement. The timing advantage is stronger for speculative content, and the AI-dominant penalty is stronger for experienced creators. Timing and mode further operate as substitutes, with later adoption producing the greatest engagement premium when creators preserve human-dominant production. Simulation analyses translate these findings into a strategic matrix based on content type and creator experience. The results challenge the industry view that creators should use GenAI early and extensively, showing instead that audience engagement depends on matching adoption timing and collaboration mode to creators' audience relationships and creative domains.
