nodes.title: The Pilot Was Never the Product
nodes.abstract:
If your organization already has someone directing AI agents, that person ships faster than your staffed teams. Probably not as fast as they could, though: directing agents well is its own skill, and few people have it yet. The question that follows is the same: how do we get more of that speed. That is the wrong question. The right one is what the work left behind. The most valuable thing that person produced is not the software, and most organizations are about to throw it away. Speed is the part everyone sees; the handoff decides whether any of it was real. You're already feeling a version of this: a mandate from above to show AI results, a compliance function beside you that says no by default, and a pilot nobody can evaluate.

I was that person. In three months, working alone inside a regulated federal healthcare operation, I built a platform and, on it, a product identifying other health insurance coverage, built to drive cost avoidance and recovery. It hasn't reached production yet: the rollout is deliberately careful, which means deliberately slow. One person directed a set of AI agents organized like a team, with defined roles and handoffs. Karna's governance process certified the work PHI-free before real data was involved; an independent review is scheduled before production.

I designed the system to document everything, on purpose. What I underestimated was how much that discipline would end up mattering.

An agent cannot infer what a colleague infers. A new engineer reads half a design document, fills in the rest from experience, asks three questions in the hallway. An agent has no hallway, nothing to fill in from. So the architecture, coding philosophy, control mechanisms, and workflow had to be explicit before any code existed. Because the work does not proceed otherwise.

A staffed team can revise a plan as the work slowly reveals its gaps. Agents move too fast for that: by the time a planning gap shows up, it is already built. So the planning has to be right before anything starts, not adjusted as you go.

Most organizations have spent years trying to get engineers to write that material before code: review gates, templates, definitions of done. It does not hold: for people, documentation is optional. This is the first arrangement I have worked in where it is not.

Then the same thing happened again, one level up. Before anyone else could join, the rules had to exist on paper: a risk assessment, a tiered access model, a certification path people complete before they earn access. All of it was drafted and submitted for committee review before most of the people it governs went through it. My manager and I cleared the same checkpoint; a third colleague has since started the path. The readiness material existed before the readiness question did.

That's the finding, and like any single case, it has real limits.

What transferred is the system. What has not been tested is the role. The speed came from absence: no division of work to negotiate, no onboarding, nobody to bring along. Those are not efficiency gains, they are the defining conditions of a pilot. It also came from skill: extensive personal practice directing these systems. The agents gave back the specification, not a second person who can direct them.

That is what we will be measuring. A technical lead directs people who infer intent, push back, and correct them. Directing agents is specification under total literalism, with none of that return signal. Our correction is designed rather than proven: put a second operator on the work from week one, directing alongside, rather than reading documentation after the fact. One colleague is the first test of it.

One open question a single case can't fully settle: how much of this came from the agents, and how much just from working alone. I've worked mostly solo before, across earlier technical roles, and documentation was never this heavy. That's suggestive, not proof.

Here is why that should matter most to the most constrained people in this room. Agents and auditors want the same artifact: intent written down before action. The regulated organizations everyone assumes will adopt agents last are already fluent in the only discipline that makes agents safe.

The generalizable claim is about evaluation and staffing, not technology. Assess an agent-accelerated pilot: speed tells you little, artifacts tell you a great deal. Ask what the pilot produced besides working software. A pilot run by one operator has to produce a full specification, an asset most organizations don't credit. Then ask who runs this next, not who maintains it. If one person and their agents produced this, you can't hire your way to more of it: that skill isn't on the job market yet. You grow it in someone, the way the certification path above does; you don't recruit it.

I am a Data Science Program Manager at Karna, a healthcare and regulated-industry analytics consultancy, forward deployed into the client's operation. Fifteen years in operations where being wrong has consequences: experimental physics, critical infrastructure, utility and grid analytics, and federal healthcare data. PhD in physics with a CERN publication, MBA from Fisher, two patents, and the person who introduced agentic AI development at Karna.

The most valuable thing the agents produced was never in the codebase. It was the written rules that let the next person start, and we had them before we knew who that person would be.

nodes.title: Kingmaking: How Venture Capitalists Pick Artificial Intelligence Winners
nodes.abstract:
Motivation. The cost of training a competitive general purpose model has risen by roughly two orders of magnitude. A venture intending to compete at the frontier must now raise several hundred million dollars before it has a product, a customer, or evidence that its approach works. This changes the shape of the financing problem, not only its scale. The capital must arrive early and in one piece, and the information that would justify it arrives only after it has been spent.

The consequence for market structure is arithmetic rather than behavioural. A fund observing the customary diversification covenant of about twelve percent of committed capital needs roughly three and a third billion dollars under management to place four hundred million into a single company. Very few venture partnerships clear that bar, so the set of investors able to finance a frontier entrant is small for reasons unrelated to the merits of any team. Because that set decides before the product market can express any preference, the competitive map of the sector is drawn by a few general partners. This paper calls that act kingmaking and asks when it produces a better set of firms than the alternative.

The obvious answer is not clearly right. Concentration is normally treated as a distortion, on the reasoning that more independent participants explore more of the opportunity set. That depends on participants being wrong in different directions. In artificial intelligence they read the same benchmark tables, hire from the same laboratories and attend the same conferences, which is a consequential deviation from what the argument requires.

Methodology. The paper is theoretical, with a calibrated numerical illustration and a measurement design built on existing data. Candidate ventures require an indivisible fixed outlay representing the first informative trial, and fund sizes follow a Pareto upper tail. Participation requires that a fund's diversification covenant permit a cheque of the required size, which yields a closed form for the number of qualifying allocators.

Allocation is modelled as competition in a common value environment, since a frontier venture is worth roughly the same to any investor able to finance it. Price decomposes into three components: the rational bid, which conditions on the informational content of winning; a premium from the fund's contractual deployment clock, grounded in the literature on fee structures and implicit compensation through future fundraising; and an error term for incomplete correction of adverse selection, formalised through cursed equilibrium.

Selection quality is analysed by splitting each investor's assessment into a component common to everyone evaluating a venture and a genuinely private one. Standard aggregation results give the effective number of independent screens as a function of headcount and belief correlation. Welfare separates pecuniary transfers between entrepreneurs and limited partners from real resource allocation. All propositions are proved formally, and parameters come from customary covenant terms, typical syndicate sizes and standard characterisations of private capital concentration.

Findings. The number of investors able to finance an entrant alone falls as the fixed cost raised to the power of minus the tail exponent of the fund size distribution. With an exponent near one and a half, doubling the fixed cost removes about two thirds of the possible backers and a tenfold increase removes more than ninety five percent. Syndication shifts the schedule outward without changing its slope, because coordination is costly and bounded in the number of parties. Under representative parameters the count falls from effectively unconstrained at application layer costs to single figures at frontier costs, or roughly forty with generous syndication.

The second result concerns price. Rational bidders shade downward as competition rises, because winning against more rivals is worse news, while the deployment clock and cursedness push the other way. Since the three components respond differently to the number of bidders, the sign of the price response to competition identifies which dominates. Practitioners report that competition raises prices and auction theory says rational bidders lower them. That disagreement is usually treated as a puzzle. Here it is the measurement.

The third result concerns the quality of the funded set. Belief correlation caps the number of independent views at the reciprocal of the correlation coefficient, however many investors participate, so a diffuse market delivers far less exploration than its headcount suggests. Concentration improves the funded set when the skill advantage of the few outweighs the information lost through fewer independent views, and the required advantage falls sharply as correlation rises. The framework therefore does not conclude that concentration is harmful. It concludes that the diffuse alternative is worth less than assumed, and that the case for concentration rests on whether the few allocators genuinely screen better.

The fourth result moves inside the funded firm. Deployment pressure delivers capital in larger tranches than milestones justify, and the excess converts mechanically into irreversible commitment, since a venture that raises more than it needs signs a compute contract rather than holding cash. Such ventures should pivot less, fail later and fail larger, which differs from failing more often and is testable without return data. Welfare turns on two channels of opposite sign, and the conditions under which concentration dominates hold at the frontier and fail in the application layer, yielding a split within the sector rather than a verdict on large funds.

Implications. For founders, modest reductions in initial compute requirements may widen the financing set by more than they cost in capability, and terms depend on where a prospective backer sits in its investment period. For limited partners, the analysis points at the fee base rather than the carry structure, and at staggering investment periods across a portfolio to decorrelate deployment clocks. For incumbents, the entrant set in any segment can be forecast from the cost of a first trial, without firm level information. For competition authorities, access to compute is competition policy, since anything reducing that cost widens the entrant set with a large multiplier without intervening in capital markets. The paper closes with three indicators constructible from existing data, and with predictions that would falsify the framework.

nodes.title: The AI Bullwhip Effect: Operations in AI Model Marketplace
nodes.abstract: The rapid growth of generative artificial intelligence has given rise to AI model marketplaces that facilitate the development, sharing, and adoption of fine-tuned models. We study whether these platforms generate an AI bullwhip effect, whereby fluctuations in downstream engagement are amplified into upstream model production. Using a panel dataset from a leading AI model marketplace, we link model releases and adoption to image-level engagement and estimate a structural model of fine-tuner development decisions. Demand expectations follow a Martingale Model of Forecast Evolution, allowing us to separate responses to anticipated demand from responses to unexpected demand news. We find that fine-tuners respond strongly to positive demand shocks and that adjustment frictions create persistence in development activity. Together, these forces transform short-lived engagement shocks into larger, delayed, and more persistent fluctuations in model supply. As model development consumes substantial computational and energy resources, such amplification can lead to redundant development and excess compute use. Our findings highlight platform information design as a potential lever for mitigating supply-side volatility while preserving incentives for innovation.

nodes.title: Integrating AI in Teaching Business Stats / Analytics To Elevate Critical Thinking, Personalized Learning, and Engagement.
nodes.affiliation: The Ohio State University, Fisher College of Business
nodes.abstract:
The advancement of AI is rapidly reshaping the landscape across all sectors. We are living in an era where almost everyone has access to AI in their pockets. In academia, the key question is: How do we use AI ethically in ways that enhance critical thinking, personalized learning, and student engagement?

AI offers several opportunities to improve course design and assignment development in Business Statistics and Analytics classrooms. At the same time, it presents significant challenges, particularly when students use AI as an answer machine for take-home assignments, projects, and online exams. Despite the use of lockdown browsers and honorlock systems, significant number of students are finding ways to use AI to achieve near-perfect scores without developing a meaningful understanding of statistical concepts, tools, and outputs. As a result, they may lack the ability to explain and interpret results or make appropriate decisions and conclusions based on their analyses.
These challenges require educators to rethink how learning is designed and assessed. In this talk, I will discuss practical approaches for integrating AI into teaching while maintaining statistical rigor and fostering genuine student learning and understanding.

I hope attendees will leave with practical strategies and examples for designing AI-integrated activities that promote critical thinking, learning, and engagement in Business Statistics and Analytics classrooms.

nodes.title: Artificial Intelligence Investments and Expertise Erosion
nodes.abstract: We study the feedback between automation and expertise accumulation. Building on Autor and Thompson's (2025) "expertise framework", we develop an overlapping- generations model with endogenous on-the-job learning. Automation reduces learning in entry-level tasks, slowing expertise acquisition and worsening the economy's exper- tise distribution. Yet we show that pre-existing automation decreases firms' willingness to pay for improvements in automation: such improvements benefit occupations requir- ing high human expertise, while the supply of high-expertise workers declines with prior automation. This weakens the dynamic complementarity between automation and expertise-substituting technologies. We then endogenize automation and show that no degree of competition among AI producers eliminates the erosion externality. When the depreciation rate is sufficiently high, the optimal policy taxes their investment.

nodes.title: Narrowing the Extraversion Advantage: AI-Assisted Upward Voice and Supervisor-Rated Communication Competence
nodes.affiliation: The Ohio state University - Fisher College of Business
nodes.abstract:
Extraversion confers a small but persistent workplace advantage, particularly in interpersonal and performance-related domains (Wilmot et al., 2019). At the same time, artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming part of human-to-human communication. AI-mediated communication allows a computational agent to modify, augment, or generate messages to help a communicator accomplish interpersonal goals (Hancock et al., 2020). Recent theory further suggests that AI can reshape both what people say and how they say it through affordances such as co-creation and adaptability (Zhu et al., 2026). We develop a compensatory communication scaffold argument. Specifically, AI may be especially useful for employees lower in extraversion when they prepare to speak up to supervisors because it can provide private assistance with wording, framing, timing, and situational fit. This possibility is consequential because managers evaluate not only how often employees speak up, but also how effectively they communicate their ideas, and higher-quality voice is associated with more favorable managerial evaluations (Brykman & Raver, 2021).
We examine this argument across two complementary field studies. Study 1 used time-lagged employee data (N = 164) to test a broader compensatory pathway. AI-mediated communication use positively predicted AI competence (β = .479, p < .001), and the interaction between AI communication use and extraversion was negative (β = −.135, p = .029), indicating that the relationship between AI communication use and competence became stronger as extraversion decreased. AI competence, in turn, positively predicted later AI-enabled innovative work behavior (β = .627, p < .001). The index of moderated mediation was significant (index = −.085, 95% CI [−.163, −.005]). Because the competence construct in this study captures broader AI competence rather than interpersonal communication competence, we treat Study 1 as converging evidence for the compensatory logic rather than as an exact test of the focal upward-communication mechanism.
Study 2 provides a more direct, multisource test using matched employee-supervisor data. We focus on a four-item measure of AI-assisted upward voice preparation, capturing employees' use of AI before sharing new ideas, making recommendations, expressing work-related opinions, and suggesting procedural changes to their supervisor. In the focal sample (N = 90), AI voice communication use interacted with supervisor-rated employee extraversion to predict supervisor-rated communication competence, b = −.290, p = .005. The interaction remained significant using HC3 robust standard errors, p = .033. The relationship between AI voice use and communication competence became more favorable as employee extraversion decreased. Supervisor-rated communication competence was also positively associated with supervisor-rated innovative behavior. Supplemental analyses further indicated that communication competence was positively associated with leadership-promotion potential. Because these downstream supervisor evaluations were collected from the same source at the same time, however, we treat them as consequential correlates rather than as strong causal evidence.
Together, the studies suggest that the consequences of workplace AI use depend not only on what task AI performs, but also on who uses it and for what interpersonal purpose. This extends research showing heterogeneous returns to AI. Generative AI can compress performance differences in some work settings, whereas other evidence suggests stronger augmentation among already higher-skilled employees (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2024). Our findings identify a different source of heterogeneity, employee extraversion, and shift attention from task productivity toward interpersonal evaluation. The contribution is therefore not simply that AI improves communication. Rather, AI may alter how personality translates into socially consequential workplace perceptions by providing a private scaffold before upward voice occurs. Practically, AI-based communication support may broaden whose ideas can be expressed effectively to supervisors. A follow-up multi-wave dyadic study is designed to separate employee-reported AI voice use from later supervisor evaluations and to account for baseline communication competence and actual voice behavior, providing a stronger confirmatory test of the proposed compensatory mechanism.

Annals of the International Communication Association. Advance online publication. doi:10.1093/anncom/wlag029.

nodes.title: Toward a Manipulable Taxonomy of Product-Specific Aesthetic Dimensions
nodes.abstract:
Text-to-image generation gives designers a fast way to explore product aesthetics, but only if they
know which words reliably change how a product looks. We develop a computational method for
building product-specific taxonomies of aesthetic descriptors around three constructs: applicability
(whether a descriptor shifts a product's visual representation), prototypicality (whether the descrip-
tor already describes the category's default appearance), and orthogonality (whether a dimension
can be varied independently of the others). We measure all three through CLIP embedding shifts,
using difference vectors to remove contamination from the shared product-category term. Using
dining chairs as the focal illustration, we build the full taxonomy pipeline and then field a choice-
based conjoint study (n = 101; 2,020 choices) that reveals a sharp divergence: the descriptors that
shift a product's appearance the most are among the descriptors consumers like least. Extend-
ing the analysis to 100 product categories, we find that the taxonomy's six higher-order dimen-
sions replicate across categories, but the specific descriptor best representing a dimension changes
from category to category-generalization happens at the dimension level, not the descriptor level.
These results motivate a revision of the constructs: we recast each dimension as a transformation
axis recovered by clustering embedding residuals across products, converting applicability from an
ordinal score into a signed, continuously adjustable magnitude. Generating 20,289 images with a
CLIP-conditioned diffusion decoder, we find that a descriptor's measured applicability lands inside
the range where the manipulated product is still recognizable, about a third of the way to where it
dissolves. When two dimensions are manipulated at once, most pairs can be dialed together but
a minority interfere strongly-and the inexpensive embedding-space orthogonality screen predicts
that interference only weakly. We close with the design of planned replication studies and a discussion of future research plans.

nodes.title: Governing Human-AI Co-Creation: Capability, Opacity, and the Economics of Oversight
nodes.abstract:
Firms increasingly deploy generative AI alongside human workers, expanding workers' responsibilities from producing output to also reviewing, validating, and correcting AI-generated content. This shift makes human oversight a central mechanism of responsible AI governance. Yet human oversight is not automatically effective: AI systems can produce fluent and plausible outputs that are difficult for humans to evaluate. In many knowledge-work settings, including software development, consulting, auditing, healthcare, legal drafting, and customer service, the risk is not merely that AI makes errors, but that those errors are embedded in output that appears polished and credible. As a result, firms face a governance problem: they must decide not only whether to keep humans in the loop, but how to design the loop so that human attention is allocated effectively.

We study this problem by developing an analytical model of human-AI co-creation. In our setting, a firm deploys an AI system and relies on a human worker to both produce output and oversee AI-generated work. The firm chooses a governance policy consisting of review frequency, oversight incentives, and productive-effort incentives. The worker observes these choices and responds by choosing productive effort and oversight depth. AI capability affects the firm through two channels. First, more capable AI increases the scale and value of AI-enabled production. Second, more capable AI can make errors harder to detect because its output is more fluent, coherent, and persuasive. We call this second channel capability-induced opacity. This creates a fundamental trade-off: AI capability raises productivity, but it may also increase the burden and reduce the effectiveness of responsible oversight.

We first consider a complete-information Stackelberg game as the baseline. Specifically, the firm moves first by setting review frequency and effort-based compensation, and the worker moves second by choosing productive effort and oversight depth. This structure captures a common feature of AI-enabled work: the firm can design incentives and review policies, but the worker ultimately determines how much effort to devote to production and how carefully to scrutinize AI output. We then consider an extension in which oversight depth is hidden from the firm. In this moral-hazard extension, the firm cannot directly contract on review depth and can instead motivate oversight only through rewards for verified error detection. The comparison between these two regimes allows us to isolate how hidden oversight changes the economics of responsible AI governance.

Our analysis yields several results that are surprising relative to the common intuition that more AI capability and more human review are always beneficial. First, review frequency and oversight depth are substitutes from the worker's perspective. When the firm requires AI output to be reviewed more frequently, each review becomes less deep unless the firm adjusts incentives. However, aggregate effective oversight can still increase with review frequency when the gain in coverage dominates the decline in per-review depth. This result shows that firms face a nontrivial design choice: reviewing more outputs is not equivalent to reviewing them more carefully.

Second, the optimal governance policy depends critically on the costs of scaling review. As the organizational cost of review frequency increases, the firm reduces the fraction of AI output that is reviewed. Thus, responsible AI governance is costly to scale, especially when review requires coordination, workflow interruptions, documentation, escalation, or managerial attention. This result helps explain why firms may formally adopt human-in-the-loop policies while still relying on selective or shallow oversight in practice.

Third, higher AI capability does not always improve firm performance. When AI capability primarily increases productive output, the marginal value of oversight rises because there is more AI-enabled work to protect. However, when capability-induced opacity is sufficiently strong, more capable AI reduces the effectiveness of each unit of human review. In that case, a more capable AI system can generate greater governance burden and may even lower firm profit. This result identifies a mechanism through which a less capable but more governable AI system can dominate a more capable but opaque one.

Fourth, in the hidden-oversight extension, monitoring infrastructure becomes central to responsible AI governance. When oversight depth is not directly observable, the firm's ability to induce careful review depends on whether caught errors can be verified and rewarded. Better monitoring quality increases hidden oversight, while weak verifiability reduces the firm's ability to motivate careful review. The extension therefore shows that governance infrastructure and AI capability can be complements: firms adopting more capable AI may also need stronger systems for verification, audit trails, escalation, and feedback.

The paper contributes to the analytical literature on co-creation and the emerging literature on responsible AI operations. Unlike traditional co-creation models in which all co-creators are strategic human or organizational actors, our setting features a non-strategic but opaque technology that changes both productivity and governability. The results show that responsible AI governance is not a binary choice between human review and no human review. Its effectiveness depends on the joint design of review frequency, oversight depth, incentives, monitoring quality, and AI capability.

nodes.title: Outsourcing Morality: How AI Labels in Marketing Communication Change Perceptions of Firm Morality
nodes.abstract:
In 2025, Aerie, a sister company of American Eagle relaunched its "100 Percent Aerie Real" pledge, publicly recommitting to never using AI to generate or alter bodies in its images. The brand's sales climbed 23% year over year following the relaunch. Equinox paired distorted AI-generated bodies with plain human portraits in its "Question Everything But Yourself" campaign, and Almond Breeze mined the same tension for comedy in a Jonas Brothers ad built around the tagline "No AI Needed." Across categories, many brands have been converging on a common strategy: publicly declaring that their content is AI-Free.

With the increase in use of generative AI in marketing communications, firms face a new disclosure dilemma. Regulatory and consumer pressure has pushed many platforms and firms toward disclosing AI-generated content (AIGC) by default. Existing research on algorithm aversion has focused on whether consumers penalize firms for using AI (Longoni et al. 2019; Castelo et al. 2019) and on the costs of disclosure itself. For example, recent work shows AI disclosures on social media erode the perceived effort behind the content and in turn reduce consumer engagement (Carney et al. 2026). This raises an important question for firms: beyond disclosing AI use, can firms benefit by declaring the absence of AI?

Across four experiments, we show that explicitly labeling firm marketing communications as AI-free, compared to disclosing AI use or providing no information about how the content is generated, increases consumers' perceptions of firm morality and, in turn, purchase intentions from the firm. This effect is driven by reduced perceptions that the firm is outsourcing its moral responsibility to a machine.

Study 1 (preregistered; n = 602) tested the main effect using an email advertisement of a fictional clothing brand. Participants on CloudResearch Connect were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: the ad was labeled as AI-generated, AI-free, or no information was given about how it was created (control). Participants then rated the firm's perceived morality using a five-item scale (α = .96). Condition significantly predicted perceived morality, F(2, 599) = 22.61, p < .001, ηp² = .07. Consumers rated the firm as more moral in the AI-free condition (M = 5.08) than in the control (M = 4.69, p < .001) or AI condition (M = 4.30, p < .001).

Study 2 (n = 453) conceptually replicated this effect to a press release by a fictional luggage brand and tested whether perceived morality drives downstream purchase intentions. Participants were randomly assigned to an AI-generated, AI-free, or control press release condition, then reported purchase intentions and perceived firm morality. Condition again affected both morality, F(2, 450) = 9.57, p < .001, ηp² = .04 and purchase intentions, F(2, 450) = 7.77, p < .001, ηp² = .03. A mediation analysis (PROCESS Model 4, 5,000 bootstrap samples) showed that perceived morality significantly mediated the effect of condition on purchase intentions for both the control-versus-AI contrast (indirect effect = .20, 95% CI [.003, .41]) and the AI-free-versus-AI contrast (indirect effect = .43, 95% CI [.23, .65]). 

Study 3 (n = 601) tested the proposed mechanism directly. Participants on Connect saw the same press release from Study 2 and additionally rated the extent to which the firm was outsourcing its moral obligations to a machine as well as the extent to which the firm's practices caused harm to people through job loss. Condition significantly affected perceived morality, F(2, 598) = 19.74, p < .001, ηp² = .06, outsourcing morality, F(2, 598) = 26.40, p < .001, ηp² = .08, and perceived harm from job loss, F(2, 598) = 61.71, p < .001, ηp² = .17. When both variables were entered as parallel mediators of condition's effect on perceived morality, only outsourcing morality emerged as a significant mediator across all three pairwise contrasts - AI vs. control (indirect effect = .11, 95% CI [.03, .21]), AI vs. AI-free (indirect effect = .14, 95% CI [.04, .27]), and control vs. AI-free (indirect effect = .04, 95% CI [.00, .10]), while the indirect effect through perceived harm from job loss was not significant. This indicates that consumers do not penalize AI-generated content primarily because they believe it was made at the expense of a human worker's employment, but because it signals that the firm is using technology to avoid taking moral responsibility.

Study 4 (n = 568) tested whether the AI-free label's benefit depends on a firm's prior moral history. Using a 2 (ad type: AI-free vs. control) × 2 (firm morality: high vs. low) between-subjects design, we found a significant Ad Type × firm morality interaction on both perceived morality, F(1, 564) = 9.38, p = .002, ηp² = .016, and purchase intentions, F(1, 562) = 4.06, p = .044, ηp² = .007. Among firms with a low prior moral history, an AI-free label significantly boosted perceived morality (3.09 vs. 3.92, p < .001) and purchase intentions (2.96 vs. 3.55, p < .001) relative to control. Among firms with a high prior moral history, the AI-free label had no significant effect on either perceived morality (5.90 vs. 6.09, p = .205) or purchase intentions (5.78 vs. 5.90, p = .449). An AI-free label helps when a firm's moral standing is otherwise low, and offers no returns once a firm has already established a strong moral reputation.

Together, these findings show that explicitly communicating that marketing content is AI-free can increase consumers' perceptions of firm morality and, in turn, their willingness to purchase from the firm. Importantly, the effect is not simply about consumers disliking AI-generated content; relative to a control condition in which firms provide no information about how their content was created, an AI-free claim provides a moral signal. This signal operates by reducing the perception that the firm is outsourcing its moral responsibility to a machine. As AI becomes increasingly common, explicitly signaling that a firm has chosen not to use AI may offer a unique way for firms to strengthen perceptions of their moral character, particularly when those perceptions are in need of repair.

nodes.title: The Selection Behind the Penalty: Strategic and Mandatory AI Disclosure in Music Streaming
nodes.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used to assist the creation of cultural goods, and policymakers have responded by requiring that AI use be disclosed. Within roughly two years, mandatory AI-content labeling moved from proposal to law across the largest media markets: China's labeling rules took effect in 2025, the European Union's AI Act will require the disclosure of synthetic content under Article 50, and platforms from YouTube to the major music services have adopted policies of their own. The premise animating this wave is that AI involvement is a liability to be revealed: labeled AI content is observed to underperform, so a rule forcing its disclosure is presumed to tax the artists who use these tools. But when disclosure is voluntary, the observed gap between disclosed and concealed AI work blends two very different things: how listeners respond to a label, and which songs artists choose to reveal in the first place. If artists conceal precisely the songs that disclosure would cost the most, the raw gap mostly reflects that choice rather than the label's effect. Separating the two is a first-order question for theory and policy. It requires observing an artist's true AI use, including what was concealed, together with a change in disclosure independent of the artist's choice.

We study two disclosure regimes on a major music-streaming platform with an integrated generative-AI music tool. For more than two years, disclosure was voluntary: an artist who made a song with the tool could credit it to listeners or stay silent, and many stayed silent. Two features of the setting make the decomposition possible. First, we observe ground-truth AI use from the platform's back end, including songs that used AI but were never disclosed to listeners, so we see concealment directly rather than inferring it from what artists say. Second, we can hold the work fixed-the same audio, the same artist, the same song, observed both before and after a label is imposed on it. The two regimes do different jobs. In the voluntary regime we model which AI songs artists choose to credit and measure the raw conceal-versus-credit performance gap within each artist's own catalog. The mandatory regime supplies the missing counterfactual: the platform began attaching a listener-facing AI label to eligible AI songs on September 2025, but the label applied only to songs published on or after an April 2025 eligibility cutoff. Otherwise-similar concealed songs published just before the cutoff were never labeled, while those published just after were labeled at the shock. Comparing the two cohorts through the shock in a difference-in-differences design, with the song held fixed, recovers listeners' causal response to an AI label. This is the field counterpart of laboratory experiments that randomize AI disclosure on a fixed work, now with the selection margin observed rather than assumed away.

Four results follow. First, we find that artists who adopt the AI tool sharply increase their output relative to matched non-adopters. Second, disclosure is strategic rather than idiosyncratic. Crediting tracks the song and the artist in interpretable ways: songs that enter a genre new to the artist, that carry a larger production team, or in which the artist's own contribution is more visible are the ones more likely to credit the AI, while songs in the artist's habitual genres are concealed. Third, the raw voluntary gap observed is large. Within an artist's own catalog, concealed AI songs outperform credited ones by roughly 1.2 log points in plays, about a threefold difference. Fourth, the causal penalty is small relative to the raw voluntary gap. When the mandate forces disclosure onto a previously concealed song, its plays fall by only about five percent. The effect operates at discovery-fewer listeners begin the song, while completion and post-listening engagement are unchanged-and it falls unevenly, concentrated among lower- and middle-tier artists and near zero for the established. Setting the two regimes side by side, even taking the causal estimate at its largest and the voluntary gap at face value, the genuine listener response accounts for at most a few percent of the observed conceal-credit gap. The overwhelming remainder is selection. The raw voluntary comparison overstates the causal penalty of disclosure by more than an order of magnitude.

The results carry a direct policy reading and a conceptual contribution. For policy, mandatory AI labeling is debated as though it levied a heavy tax on the artists who comply, a presumption the raw disclosure gap appears to license. Our estimates suggest the tax is modest, that it operates at discovery rather than in how listeners engage with a song they have chosen to play, and that it is regressive: the cost falls on the newer and smaller artists whose audiences have the least other information, and is near zero for the established. Transparency rules should be judged against the small penalty that disclosure actually imposes, not the far larger one that artists were avoiding. Conceptually, the paper connects the economics of voluntary disclosure with the behavioral research on AI aversion. The classic prediction of disclosure theory is unraveling toward full revelation; we show why it reverses for AI authorship. Because AI use is not verifiable to listeners and the authenticity penalty it carries is real, sticky, and never good news for the discloser, silence rather than revelation is the equilibrium, and voluntary disclosure sorts songs rather than informing listeners. This complements, rather than competes with, both the laboratory studies that cleanly identify the listener response and the field studies that observe real disclosure choices: our design adds the concealment and the within-work counterfactual that a decomposition of the market penalty requires. It reframes how the disclosure penalties documented across a fast-growing literature should be read-as compounds of listener response and artist selection, not estimates of the former alone.

nodes.title: Who Pays for the Cloud? The Impact of Data Center Entry on Grocery Purchases
nodes.affiliation: Gies College of Business, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
nodes.abstract:
In recent years, data centers have proliferated rapidly (Kearney 2024). Essential to cloud computing and artificial intelligence, data centers provide services that are consumed far beyond the communities that host them. During our 2004-2014 study period, data centers supported services like Amazon's S3 and EC2 and cloud infrastructure used by eBay (Amazon Web Services 2006; Microsoft 2010). Public debate and emerging research have largely evaluated the impact of data centers through electricity demand, utility prices, and employment (Alvarez et al. 2026; Kay, Reaser, and Taylor 2026). While important, these effects do not directly measure household response to data center entry. Household spending provides a more direct and reliable measure of household response (Dubé, Hitsch, and Rossi 2018; Scholdra et al. 2022). While data center entry can drive up costs, put pressure on households' budgets, and reduce spending, it can also create jobs and economic opportunities that increase spending.

Our paper asks three related questions: What is the effect of data center entry on local household grocery spending, including purchase frequency and basket size and composition? How do these effects evolve over time, (i.e. short-, medium-, and long-term adjustments in grocery spending)? Importantly, are the counties with the strongest response also those most likely to leverage and benefit from data center capabilities?

To answer our research questions, we combine annual establishment records from the National Establishment Time Series (NETS) with household purchase records from the 2004--2014 NielsenIQ Consumer Panel. We define entry as the first year in which a county records stable local estabilishmen classified under NAICS 518210, Data Processing, Hosting, and Related Services, between 2006 and 2014. The design includes 52 treated counties and 2,160 counties that do not record a qualifying entry. Using Callaway-Sant'Anna staggered difference-in-differences design, we estimate cohort- and time-specific treatment effects by comparing post-entry changes in treated counties with contemporaneous changes in never-treated counties. The study period gives us a clean quasi-experimental setting predating recent generative-AI-driven acceleration in data-center expansion, the current political and media salience of data centers, and the pandemic-era expansion of online grocery shopping. 

Our analysis shows several interesting results. First, we find that annual CPG spending declines by 12.3% after data center entry (SE = 0.051), which yields an average post-entry decrease of approximately $420 per household-year. Second, the decline is modest during the first three years and becomes larger and statistically significant thereafter. We provide several robustness checks, including an event study analysis shows no evidence of differential pretreatment trends in total CPG spending (p = .72). 

Our mechanism analysis further helps understand what drives the average spending declines. By decomposing spending into recorded purchase occasions and spending per occasion, we find about 27 fewer recorded occasions per household-year(decline by 16.8%), while spending per occasion does not change significantly. The recorded CPG spending decline is therefore associated with fewer recorded purchase occasions, not smaller amounts spent per occasion. Furthermore, the reduction is concentrated in lower-value purchase occasions: those under $10 fall by roughly 14 per household-year, while larger occasions change little. We find little evidence of a broad trade-down: deal purchases, coupon use, and private-label share do not change detectably. In terms of basket composition, it appears that households reduce purchases of non-food and non-discretionary categories, such as stationery, kitchen and housewares, pet and baby care, and paper products, while the purchases of storable staples such as canned goods, cereal, and frozen prepared meals do not decrease.

Finally, we ask whether places that respond most strongly also share in local economic gains. Using County Business Patterns for establishments and employment and Bureau of Economic Analysis data for per capita income, we find that in nonmetropolitan counties, annual recorded CPG spending declines by 19.8%, compared with 8.1% in metropolitan counties, while per capita income declines by 1.7% versus 1.1%. The pattern reverses for local economic expansion: metropolitan counties experience 6.1% growth in establishments and 6.4% growth in employment, compared with 1.8% and 2.2% in nonmetropolitan counties. Thus, the larger household purchasing decline appears where measured local business and employment gains are smaller. 

Overall, our research contributes in three ways. First, to our knowledge, we provide the first evidence on how data center entry affects local household consumption. Second, we contribute to the marketing research on household responses to changing economic conditions (i.e., major digital infrastructure entry) and document declines in spending driven by a reduced purchase frequency, rather than spending per occasion and product trade-down. Third, we document a mismatch between who bears the local cost of the cloud and who benefits from it; the counties and households that cut back most are not those positioned to share in data-center-related gains. Our research has several implications. For retailers and manufacturers, a decline in grocery purchases because of fewer purchase occasions has different implications relative to one driven by smaller baskets or substitution toward cheaper products; it removes the occasions on which households can be reached and converted at all. For policymakers weighing regulations, entry decisions, and host-community benefits, our results on household purchases offer a direct measure of consumer response.

References:
Alvarez, Fernando E., David Argente, Joyce Chow, and Diana Van Patten. 2026. "Data Centers and Local Economies in the Age of AI: A Shift-Share Approach." NBER Working Paper No. 35194.
Amazon Web Services. 2006. "Announcing Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2)-Beta." August 24.
Dubé, Jean-Pierre, Günter J. Hitsch, and Peter E. Rossi. 2018. "Income and Wealth Effects on Private-Label Demand: Evidence from the Great Recession." Marketing Science 37 (1): 22-53.
Kay, Owen, Robert Reaser, and Reid Taylor. 2026. "Processing Power: The Effect of Data Centers on Wholesale Electricity Markets." Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas Working Paper No. 2606.
Kearney, Laila. 2024. "Data Centers Could Use 9% of U.S. Electricity by 2030, Research Institute Says." Reuters, May 29.
Microsoft. 2010. "eBay and Microsoft Announce Cloud Computing Agreement." July 12.
Scholdra, Thomas P., Julian R. K. Wichmann, Maik Eisenbeiss, and Werner J. Reinartz. 2022. "Households Under Economic Change: How Micro- and Macroeconomic Conditions Shape Grocery Shopping Behavior." Journal of Marketing 86 (4): 95-117.

nodes.title: GOVERNING AGENTIC AI WORKFLOWS: OVERSIGHT IN AGENTIC AND ASSISTIVE MODES
nodes.abstract:
Motivation. Modern AI models can perform many discrete knowledge-work tasks accurately, yet their performance often deteriorates in multi-step workflows, where planning, tool use, execution, quality control, and revision unfold over many interdependent steps. Earlier errors propagate and make subsequent mistakes more likely. Yet worker-AI engagement patterns are often unobservable: firms may not know how carefully workers verify AI-generated outputs, when they intervene, or when they invoke AI support. The central governance challenge is therefore not simply whether to keep humans in the loop, but where to position them and how to incentivize their engagement when intermediate verification is costly and difficult to observe. We study optimal checkpoint placement-the frequency of human-AI engagement-in two workflow designs: an agentic design, in which AI executes and a human checks, and an assistive design, in which a human executes and AI checks. The agentic design captures practices such as vibe coding and agentic engineering, in which workers delegate goals to AI agents and review their outputs at selected checkpoints. The assistive design captures human-led copilot workflows, in which workers retain execution and invoke tools such as GitHub Copilot or Gemini Code Assist for verification and suggestions. Because a human remains the doer and bears more of the consequences of mistakes, managers may view the assistive design as more reliable and easier to govern. The comparison is complicated by AI's jagged intelligence-the tendency of the same AI system to perform extremely well on some tasks but poorly on others that appear similar. Humans, by contrast, tend to perform more consistently across comparable tasks. Jaggedness therefore captures variation in AI reliability across tasks, rather than simply low average accuracy: systems with the same average failure rate can generate different patterns of errors. This distinction matters because role assignment determines how jagged performance enters final outcomes and how clearly those outcomes reveal hidden engagement.
Methodology. We develop an analytical framework that jointly determines checkpoint policies, human-AI role assignments, and outcome-based incentives in a multi-step workflow. A doer, either AI or human, completes N subtasks in sequence, while a checker decides how often to inspect intermediate work. Each inspection is costly but can catch errors and trigger repairs before they propagate. A check every k tasks reduces final errors, whereas less frequent checks save oversight cost but allow errors to accumulate, increasing rework and terminal errors. We first characterize the optimal checkpoint policy when engagement is observable. This first-best policy provides the target that the firm seeks to implement when checkpoint placement is hidden. Because token-based quotas are insufficient to induce the desired engagement, we focus on outcome-based contracts. Under limited liability, the worker privately chooses when to inspect AI's intermediate output in the agentic design or invoke AI support to verify her work in the assistive design. We derive contracts implementing the firm's preferred checkpoint policy when both parties are risk neutral and when the worker alone is risk-averse.
Findings. First, the operational value of oversight is non-monotone in task difficulty. The optimal checkpoint interval is U-shaped in the doer's failure rate: it is long for easy tasks, shortest at intermediate difficulty, and lengthens again as the task becomes hard. When errors are rare, frequent review adds little value. As failures become more common, shorter intervals prevent errors from propagating across downstream steps. Beyond an interior threshold, however, repeated checks and rework become too costly relative to their corrective value, so the firm checks less often and eventually moves to an end-only check. Second, moderate AI jaggedness may approximately preserve expected final performance, but it changes the distribution of final errors differently across collaboration modes. This distinction matters once the firm must contract on final outcomes, because the shape of the distribution determines how clearly performance reveals hidden engagement. Average accuracy alone is therefore insufficient to compare the two designs.
Third, when checkpoint placement is hidden, workers choose to under-check in both designs unless given an additional incentive. The agentic worker bears the checkpoint cost but does not internalize the benefit of catching AI errors. The assistive worker bears both checkpoint and rework costs and is therefore more closely aligned with the firm, but still does not internalize the full cost of undetected final errors. Despite this stronger private-cost alignment, the assistive design can be more expensive to govern. For a risk-neutral worker with limited liability and uncapped pay, a lower-tail threshold bonus can implement the agentic first best with zero information rent. The optimal contract concentrates compensation on a rare, low-error outcome that is highly informative about human checks. By contrast, outcomes under the assistive design have bounded incentive power because changing the checkpoint interval rescales the same noisy checker realization. Any nonnegative outcome contract implementing an interior first best must satisfy a payment floor determined by AI jaggedness and task difficulty. A more jagged AI and a harder task raise this floor. If it exceeds participation compensation, the firm must pay information rent or implement a different checkpoint interval. The floor disappears at the end-only-check corner, where the firm and worker prefer the same action. Worker risk aversion further makes outcome-contingent compensation costly and generates different rent profiles across the two designs.
Implications. Common managerial intuition suggests choosing the agentic design when AI execution appears technically less costly and the assistive design when human-led work appears more reliable. Our analysis shows that this intuition is incomplete. When the contract remains constant across role assignments, stronger private-cost alignment can favor the assistive design. Once the firm tailors the optimal contract to each workflow, however, this ranking can reverse because agentic outcomes may provide sharper evidence of hidden checkpoint placement and support more targeted rewards. Firms should therefore choose workflow design and incentive contracts jointly. The preferred collaboration mode depends not only on technical production cost, average accuracy, or perceived reliability, but also on error propagation, task difficulty, AI jaggedness, human risk preferences, and the cost of inducing hidden engagement. Assistive workflows' perceived reliability does not necessarily make them easier or less costly to govern in practice.
